narrative:
The model determined that you have a 36% chance of being a bad credit risk. Because this probability exceeded the bank's approval threshold, your loan application was denied.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this outcome were the length of the loan you requested, the status of your checking account, and your credit history. The short eight-month duration of your requested loan was the single biggest reason the model leaned toward approval. In contrast, your checking account status of less than zero DM pushed the prediction noticeably toward denial. This is relatively uncommon; only 12.6% of approved applicants show a negative balance, while most have either no account or positive balances. Your credit history marked as "critical or other credits" also worked against you, though its negative influence was slightly smaller than the checking-account effect.

Taken together, the unfavorable checking-account status and credit-history signals outweighed the positive effect of the short loan term, tipping the model past the approval line.

You should focus on two practical next steps. First, bring your checking account into positive territory and maintain it that way for several months. Second, review your credit report to understand and resolve any past issues that created the "critical" rating. Once those areas improve, reapply; the model will then view your profile more favorably.
